arXiv:2506.08329v3 [cond-mat.dis-nn] 29 Oct 2025

Neuralized Fermionic Tensor Networks for Quantum Many-Body Systems

Si-Jing Du Email: sdu2@caltech.edu Affiliation: Division of Engineering and Applied Science, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA    Ao Chen Affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA    Garnet Kin-Lic Chan Email: gkc1000@gmail.com Affiliation: Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, USA
Abstract

We describe a class of neuralized fermionic tensor network states (NN-fTNS) that introduce non-linearity into fermionic tensor networks through configuration-dependent neural network transformations of the local tensors. The construction uses the fTNS algebra to implement a natural fermionic sign structure and is compatible with standard tensor network algorithms, but gains enhanced expressivity through the neural network parametrization. Using the 1D and 2D Fermi-Hubbard models as benchmarks, we demonstrate that NN-fTNS achieve order of magnitude improvements in the ground-state energy compared to pure fTNS with the same bond dimension, and can be systematically improved through both the tensor network bond dimension and the neural network parametrization. Compared to existing fermionic neural quantum states (NQS) based on Slater determinants and Pfaffians, NN-fTNS offer a physically motivated alternative fermionic structure. Furthermore, compared to such states, NN-fTNS naturally exhibit improved computational scaling and we demonstrate a construction that achieves linear scaling with the lattice size.

Introduction

Finding compact representations of quantum many-body wavefunctions remains a central challenge in the study of strongly correlated quantum systems [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. In previous work [6], we introduced tensor network function (TNF) representations of quantum states. These expand the well-known tensor network states (TNS) [7, 2, 3, 8, 9] to more general functions of the input, capturing new kinds of physics such as volume law entanglement, while still allowing for a connection to and the reuse of existing tensor network algorithms.

In the current work, we are concerned with describing fermionic quantum many-body problems which have a sign structure in the wavefunction. Fermionic TNS [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18] utilize a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} graded tensor product to encode the sign structure and have been demonstrated to be a powerful Ansatz for many problems [19, 15, 20, 21, 22, 16, 23]. At the same time, TNFs allow for substantial flexibility in function design, including the incorporation of nonlinearity into the tensor network computational graph. Motivated by both these observations, we propose a class of fermionic TNFs enhanced with neural network-induced nonlinearity, which we denote NN-fTNS. NN-fTNS serve as a bridge between pure tensor networks and pure neural networks, combining the conceptual advantages of fermionic tensor networks with the expressive flexibility of neural networks. While hybrid Ansätze [24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29] combining tensor networks and neural networks have been explored in bosonic spin systems [25, 26, 29], here we demonstrate the power of this hybrid approach in the fermionic setting, in the framework of tensor network functions, where the tensor network arguably plays a more critical role. In particular, in the study of fermionic neural network quantum states (NQS) [4, 5, 30, 31, 32], it is essential to incorporate a proper physical bias towards the correct fermionic sign structure. Most conventional fermionic NQS approaches rely on a mean-field Slater determinant or Pfaffian to provide this bias [5, 31, 32, 33, 30]. NN-fTNS use the fTNS computational graph arising from the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} graded tensor product as the physical bias for the neural network function, providing a conceptually distinct option from existing mean-field based NQS.

Fermionic TNS and neural network configuration dependence

For a quantum many-body system defined on a lattice with NN sites, given a local dd-dimensional on-site basis set |ni⟩|n_{i}\rangle, many TNS can be defined as the following general form [2, 3],

|ψ⟩=∑{α},n1,…,nNTα1n1​…​TαNnN​|n1⟩⊗|n2⟩⊗…⊗|nN⟩|\psi\rangle=\sum_{\{\alpha\},n_{1},...,n_{N}}T^{n_{1}}_{\alpha_{1}}...T^{n_{N}}_{\alpha_{N}}|n_{1}\rangle\otimes|n_{2}\rangle\otimes...\otimes|n_{N}\rangle (1)

where ⊗\otimes denotes the tensor product of the local basis states. For simplicity, we will denote the many-body product basis state as |n⟩=|n1⟩⊗|n2⟩⊗…⊗|nN⟩|n\rangle=|n_{1}\rangle\otimes|n_{2}\rangle\otimes...\otimes|n_{N}\rangle. The quantum wavefunction amplitude ⟨n|ψ⟩\langle n|\psi\rangle in Eq. (1) is decomposed into a product of local tensors TαiniT^{n_{i}}_{\alpha_{i}}, where αi\alpha_{i} denotes the (set of) virtual indices on each tensor, all of which are eventually traced out, shown by the summation over {α}\{\alpha\}. Each virtual index connects at most two tensors and is thus referred to as a bond, whose dimension is denoted DD. The amplitude definition in Eq. (1) involves an exponential sum over {α}\{\alpha\}, which in practice is replaced by a restricted summation ∑{α~}\sum_{\{\tilde{\alpha}\}}, defined with the aid of additional, auxiliary, tensors that map {α}→{α~}\{\alpha\}\to\{\tilde{\alpha}\} according to some contraction scheme [9, 8, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38], with an associated bond dimension χ\chi. When computing amplitudes these auxiliary tensors are amplitude dependent, and with TNFs they are considered to be an intrinsic part of the computational graph, rather than an approximation to Eq.(1), thus the tensors in a TNF are configuration dependent.

A fermionic TNS (fTNS) is similarly defined by using fermionic tensors for TαiniT_{\alpha_{i}}^{n_{i}} in Eq.(1), and changing the tensor product to a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-graded tensor product [10, 11]. A fermionic tensor is a tensor of values whose indices are considered to be fermionic modes. The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-graded algebra then takes care of the fermion anti-commutation relations by properly generating minus signs when permuting the fermionic modes. We refer the reader to Refs. [10, 11] for further technical details of fTNS. By definition, a fTNS is a natural representation of a fermionic wavefunction, and its wavefunction amplitudes are computed from the overlap with the product states of the physical fermionic modes.

To neuralize a fTNS, we make the local tensors of the fTNS configuration-dependent through an element-wise summation with an additional set of tensors generated by neural network functions, e.g. for the ii-th site tensor,

T[i]​(ni)→T[i]​(ni)+TNN[i]​(n)T^{[i]}(n_{i})\to T^{[i]}(n_{i})+T_{\text{NN}}^{[i]}(n) (2)

where the input to the neural network is the global configuration |n⟩|n\rangle (analogous to the bosonic case [26]). We then obtain a modified global configuration-dependent fTNS |Ψ⁡(n)⟩|\Psi(n)\rangle, namely a class of fermionic TNF. The amplitude of the resulting wavefunction is computed by contracting the corresponding amplitude tensor network ⟨n|Ψ⁡(n)⟩\langle n|\Psi(n)\rangle of the modified fTNS. In this work, we focus on fermionic MPS (fMPS) [20] and fPEPS (Fig.1(a)) [14, 22] as the fTNS structures for one- and two-dimensional systems, respectively, where for the contraction scheme for the fPEPS amplitudes, we employ the standard boundary MPS method [9, 8], illustrated in Fig. 1(b), with auxiliary bond dimension χ=4​D\chi=4D [19]. Each on-site tensor is assigned an independent neural network to introduce the configuration dependence. The neural network architecture used in this work consists of a self-attention block [39, 40, 41] followed by a two-layer fully connected feed-forward network, with a number of hidden neurons proportional to the fTNS bond dimension, and with all parameters real, see SM [42] for details. A schematic illustration of the computational graph for the NN-fTNS Ansatz is provided in Fig. 1(c).

Fermi-Hubbard model and VMC optimization

To demonstrate the power of the NN-fTNS Ansatz, we use variational Monte Carlo [43, 44, 45, 46] to optimize the ground states of the Fermi-Hubbard (FH) model, defined by the Hamiltonian

H=−t∑⟨i,j⟩,σ(ci,σ†cj,σ+h.c.)+U∑ini,↑ni,↓H=-t\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle,\sigma}(c_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{j,\sigma}+h.c.)+U\sum_{i}n_{i,\uparrow}n_{i,\downarrow} (3)

where ci,σ†c_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger} (ci,σc_{i,\sigma}) creates (annihilates) an electron with spin σ∈↑,↓\sigma\in{\uparrow,\downarrow} at site ii, and ni,σn_{i,\sigma} denotes the corresponding number operator. The notation ⟨i,j⟩\langle i,j\rangle denotes summation over nearest-neighbor pairs. We set t=1t=1 and U=8U=8 throughout, and consider both the 1D and 2D square lattice FH model with open boundary conditions (OBC). We sample amplitudes in the |n⟩|n\rangle basis according to |⟨n|Ψ⟩|2|\langle n|\Psi\rangle|^{2} using a Markov Chain as done in TN-VMC [6, 19, 43, 45, 46]. After suitable initialization (discussed below), the state is optimized by gradient optimization (denoted GO), see SM [42] for details.

A key advantage of the NN-fTNS hybrid structure is that it suggests an effective model initialization strategy, which consists of two components. First, we can initialize the fTNS part using standard tensor network optimization techniques [47, 48, 49, 50, 51], specifically here, the simple update (SU) imaginary time evolution method [47], to obtain a pure fTNS approximation to the ground state. Second, the neural network parameters are initialized such that they provide a small perturbation to the fTNS [42]. This combined strategy yields high-quality initial states that are suitable for subsequent global optimization of the full NN-fTNS Ansatz.

NN-fTNS for fermionic ground state energies

To first demonstrate that fTNS provide a suitable fermionic sign structure, we compare the ground state optimization performance of NN-fTNS against various other Ansätze on a small 4×24\times 2 FH square lattice with hole doping nh=1/4n_{h}=1/4; the VMC converged energy is shown as a function of the number of variational parameters in Fig. 2, and details of all Ansätze in the SM [42]; the fPEPS bond dimension is fixed to D=4D=4 in all fTNS-based models. The NN model sizes dominate the number of parameters for all Ansätze. Comparing NN-fPEPS with pure fPEPS (initialized by SU), we clearly observe that the addition of the neural network configuration dependence increases the model expressivity, allowing a further energy reduction beyond what is achieved by pure fPEPS. The pure NN Ansatz reaches a large relative energy error of approximately 30%30\% despite a large model size, demonstrating that the fTNS provides the crucial fermionic sign structure that the pure neural network fails to capture. For a further comparison, we also use a conventional neural network backflow state [5], where a Slater determinant is used to encode the fermionic sign structure (denoted as NN-SD). We implement this NN-SD calculation with two NN architectures: (1) a simple feed-forward network (NN-SD (MLP)), similar to Ref. [5], and (2) a modern Transformer [39, 52] (NN-SD (ViT)), which mimics the sophisticated NQS model structure in recent state-of-the-art work [53]. As shown in Fig. 2, while increasing the NN size reduces the NN-SD energy, the NN-fPEPS model achieves a lower relative error for a comparable number of variational parameters. Additionally, the NN-fPEPS model requires fewer VMC optimization steps to converge than the NN-SD model (see SM [42] for VMC optimization curves). To verify that the NN modulation of the fermionic bias from fTNS is important, we have also tested adding a neural network to the fPEPS through a multiplicative Jastrow factor [25, 54]. While this does improve over the pure fPEPS calculation, the improvement is quite limited, showing the importance of direct neural network modulation of the sign structure.

We next consider other 1D and 2D lattice geometries at different dopings. We compare NN-fTNS optimized by GO to fTNS optimized both by SU and with further gradient optimization. As shown in Fig. 3, the NN-fTNS Ansatz consistently achieves a substantially lower relative energy error than the pure fTNS Ansatz with the same bond dimension, demonstrating the robustness of neural network enhancement across diverse physical regimes. The fTNS-SU plateaus in accuracy at about 1% due to the known limitations of SU optimization [55], but the fTNS-GO result systematically converges to exactness with increasing DD. The NN-fTNS also systematically converges with increasing DD, maintaining a roughly constant (approximately 1-2 orders of magnitude) improvement over the the fTNS-GO result, with a NN model size that is proportional to DD. In the largest simulation shown, the 6×66\times 6 square lattice at hole doping nh=1/9n_{h}=1/9 (Fig. 3(d)), the NN-fPEPS Ansatz with bond dimension D=8D=8 surpasses the accuracy of a pure fPEPS with D=16D=16. The total number of parameters in the NN-fPEPS model with D=8D=8 is 1,647,024, fewer than the 2,230,272 parameters in the pure fPEPS with D=16D=16, despite achieving a lower energy.

In contrast, removing the fTNS bias results in significantly worse energies. A pure neural network Ansatz yields relative energy errors of 22.68% and 14.78% for the 4×44\times 4 FH model at half filling and at hole doping nh=1/8n_{h}=1/8, respectively [42], and a recent study using an autoregressive NQS without a fermionic mean-field bias for the same system at half filling reported a relative error of 8×10−38\times 10^{-3} [56], worse than our smallest NN-fPEPS calculation with bond dimension D=4D=4, which achieved a 4×10−44\times 10^{-4} relative error. Similarly, a baseline NN-SD calculation achieved relative energy errors of only 2.31% (MLP), 0.18% (ViT) at half filling and 3.18% (MLP), 0.6% (CNN [42, 57]) at nh=1/8n_{h}=1/8 [42]. These results highlight the quality of the fermionic sign structure provided by the fTNS.

Improving the NN expressivity

The data in Fig. 3 shows that increasing the bond dimension DD of the base fTNS leads to consistent improvements in energy accuracy. We next consider whether improving the neural network model similarly systematically reduces the error. As an initial test, we have increased the number of hidden neurons (denoted as WW, the layer width) in the final neural network layer of the MLP that interfaces with the tensor network. As shown in Fig. 4, wider neural network layers result in modest but consistent improvements in the converged energy. This preliminary observation suggests that NN-fTNS can also be systematically improved from the neural network side. In future work, it will be valuable to further explore how the neural network model affects the performance of NN-fTNS.

Scaling to larger systems

The cost to compute an amplitude in a NN-fTNS is O⁡(N)O(N) where NN is the system size [44, 19, 58]. This can be contrasted with the O⁡(N3)O(N^{3}) scaling for a Slater determinant or Pfaffian NQS [5]. However, in a Markov Chain VMC calculation, typically a series of related configurations are generated in a sweep [59], for example in the computation of the local energy. In a pure fTNS VMC calculation, computation can be reused (in the form of partial tensor network contraction intermediates [42]) which means that for a local Hamiltonian (such as the FH model), the cost per VMC energy and step is still O⁡(N)O(N) [60, 6]. However, the global configuration dependence of a NN-fTNS means that even local configuration changes in the amplitude lead to a global modification of the tensors, preventing re-use and leading to an O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) scaling for each VMC step. (This is related to the O⁡(N4)O(N^{4}) scaling of a VMC step with Slater determinant/Pfaffian NQS when reuse is not possible [33, 61, 32, 30]). This is illustrated in the time cost comparisons between NN-fPEPS and fPEPS for various bond dimensions DD in Fig. 5(a). Clearly, there exists a trade-off between the range of neural network-induced configuration dependence and the degree of reuse of partial tensor network contractions.

To enable reuse, we introduce a spatial cutoff to the neural network configuration dependence. Specifically, we restrict the neural network input to a given tensor to only the configuration string within a finite range RR of the tensor site. Consequently, local configuration changes induce modifications only to a fixed number of tensors in the tensor network, allowing for the reuse of partial tensor network contractions in the unaffected regions.

To illustrate the cost reduction arising from tensor network reuse in conjunction with the finite range neural network dependence, we perform VMC optimizations on a one-dimensional Hubbard chain using NN-fMPS where the NN is restricted to range RR. As anticipated and as shown in Fig. 5(b), this finite-range approach significantly reduces the computational cost scaling with system size, compared to the original (OPENR=∞)R=\infty) NN-fMPS parametrization. But notably, we find that even a minimal finite-range neural network with R=1R=1 achieves a ground-state energy accuracy that is significantly better than that of the pure fTNS, as shown in Fig. 5(b) and Fig. 5(c) for the 1D and 2D FH model, demonstrating the potential of the NN-fTNS with finite RR to scale up to large systems with a controllable computational cost.

Discussions

We have described how to augment fTNS with neural network configuration dependence. The resulting NN-fTNS are a class of fermionic TNF and we demonstrate that they achieve significant and consistent improvements over fTNS in ground-state energy simulations of the Fermi-Hubbard model. Compared to existing fermionic NQS, NN-fTNS provide a number of potential advantages, including accurate initialization states, lower computational scaling, and a new source of sign structure beyond the fermionic mean-field forms of Slater determinants and Pfaffians. The current work raises a number of open questions. One is whether, for certain Hamiltonians, entanglement-based NN-fTNS more faithfully capture the fermionic sign structure than mean-field based fermionic NQS. A natural candidate is Hamiltonians with certain topologically ordered fermionic ground-states, for which fTNS provide a compact description [20, 21, 22]. Another open direction to explore is the impact of neural network model architecture on the expressivity of NN-fTNS. We expect such questions to be addressed in future work.

Appendix S-1 S-1. Model architecture

S-1.1 NN-fTNS

Below we provide details of the model architecture used in the NN-fTNS Ansatz, as illustrated in the computational graph for the amplitude ⟨n|Ψ⟩\langle n|\Psi\rangle in Fig. S1. We emphasize that the neural network architecture employed in this study may not represent the optimal design for the NN-fTNS model, as the focus of this work is not to identify state-of-the-art neural network structures. Apart from the preliminary observation that increasing the number of hidden neurons in the MLP blocks can improve the model expressivity, it remains an open and valuable direction for future work to systematically investigate the impact of neural network architecture on the performance of NN-fTNS.

NN-fTNS computational graph We describe the computational graph shown in Fig. S1(a) from bottom to top. The local on-site configuration of the ii-th site is first encoded using a one-hot representation, where the four basis states {0,↑,↓,↑↓}\{0,\uparrow,\downarrow,\uparrow\downarrow\} are mapped to the four orthonormal unit vectors 𝐞i(j)∈ℝ4\mathbf{e}_{i}^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{4} (j=0,1,2,3j=0,1,2,3) in four-dimensional Euclidean space. The one-hot encoded on-site configuration is then embedded into a dd-dimensional feature vector (Fig.S1(b)) through a linear transformation:

fi=𝐞i(j)​Wembed∈ℝdf_{i}=\mathbf{e}_{i}^{(j)}\,W_{\mathrm{embed}}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{d} (S1)

where Wembed∈ℝ4×dW_{\mathrm{embed}}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times d} is a learnable embedding matrix. The embedded input features for the entire system are then collected into a matrix,

X=[f1,,f2,,…,,fN]𝖳∈ℝN×d.X=\bigl[f_{1},,f_{2},,\dots,,f_{N}\bigr]^{\mathsf{T}}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}. (S2)

The features XX are subsequently fed into a standard Transformer encoder, which has an analogous structure to a Vision Transformer (ViT) [52]. Specifically, XX are input into a multi-head self-attention block with residual connection [39]:

Y=X+MultiHeadSelfAttn(X)=X+Concat[Head1∥Head2∥⋯∥Headh]WO∈ℝN×dY=X+\mathrm{MultiHeadSelfAttn}(X)=X+\mathrm{Concat}\bigl[\mathrm{Head}_{1}\,\|\,\mathrm{Head}_{2}\,\|\;\cdots\;\|\mathrm{Head}_{h}\bigr]\,W^{O}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} (S3)

where WO∈ℝd×dW^{O}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a learnable on-site output projection matrix. Each attention head operates on a subspace of dimension dk=d/hd_{k}=d/h, where hh is the number of attention heads, and is computed via the standard scaled dot-product attention:

Headi=Attention⁡(Qi,Ki,Vi)=softmax⁡(Qi​Ki𝖳dk)​Vi∈ℝN×dk,\displaystyle\mathrm{Head}_{i}\;=\mathrm{Attention}(Q_{i},\,K_{i},\,V_{i})=\;\mathrm{softmax}\bigl(\frac{Q_{i}\,K_{i}^{\mathsf{T}}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\bigr)\;V_{i}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{k}}, (S4)

The query, key, and value matrices are obtained by independent linear projections of the input features:

Qi=X​WiQ∈ℝN×dk,Ki=X​WiK∈ℝN×dk,Vi=X​WiV∈ℝN×dk.\displaystyle Q_{i}\;=\;X\,W^{Q}_{i}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{k}},\quad K_{i}\;=\;X\,W^{K}_{i}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{k}},\quad V_{i}\;=\;X\,W^{V}_{i}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{k}}. (S5)

where WiQ,WiK,WiV∈ℝd×dkW_{i}^{Q},W_{i}^{K},W_{i}^{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{k}} are head-specific learnable projection matrices for the ii-th attention head. In this work, we adopt h=4h=4 attention heads with embedding dimension d=16d=16, resulting in dk=4d_{k}=4 for each head.

The output YY of the self-attention block is subsequently normalized along the feature dimension using layer normalization. The normalized features are then flattened into a one-dimensional vector yy and passed through an on-site two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) to generate the neuralized on-site tensors:

TNN[i]​(n)=LeakyRelu⁡(y​W1[i]+b1[i])​W2[i]+b2[i],T_{\mathrm{NN}}^{[i]}(n)=\mathrm{LeakyRelu}(yW_{1}^{[i]}+b_{1}^{[i]})W_{2}^{[i]}+b_{2}^{[i]}, (S6)

where W1[i]∈ℝN​d×WW_{1}^{[i]}\in\mathbb{R}^{Nd\times W}, W2[i]∈ℝW×dim(T[i])W_{2}^{[i]}\in\mathbb{R}^{W\times\dim(T^{[i]})}, b1[i]∈ℝWb_{1}^{[i]}\in\mathbb{R}^{W}, and b2[i]∈ℝdim(T[i])b_{2}^{[i]}\in\mathbb{R}^{\dim(T^{[i]})} are learnable projection matrices and biases for the MLP associated with site ii, and WW denotes the number of hidden neurons in the MLP.

The tensors in the fTNS are then modified as:

T[i]​(ni)→T[i]​(ni)+TNN[i]​(n)T^{[i]}(n_{i})\to T^{[i]}(n_{i})+T_{\text{NN}}^{[i]}(n) (S7)

which is similar to a backflow transformation [29, 26], resulting in the configuration-dependent fTNS |Ψ⁡(n)⟩|\Psi(n)\rangle. The amplitude corresponding to the configuration |n⟩|n\rangle is then obtained by contracting the single layer fTN ⟨n|Ψ⁡(n)⟩\langle n|\Psi(n)\rangle.

Model parameters initialization In VMC optimization for the NN-fTNS Ansatz, the fTNS tensors T[i]​(ni)T^{[i]}(n_{i}) are initialized using the simple update (SU) method [47], while the neural network weights in the MLP blocks (W1[i]W_{1}^{[i]} and W2[i]W_{2}^{[i]}) are initialized from a normal distribution 𝒩⁡(0,0.005)\mathcal{N}(0,0.005), ensuring that the neural network components act as small perturbations to the underlying fTNS at the beginning of the optimization.

Improving the neural network structure In the final on-site MLP following the self-attention block, the second dimension of W1[i]W_{1}^{[i]} (equivalently, the first dimension of W2[i]W_{2}^{[i]}) corresponds to the number of hidden neurons in the last layer of the neural network block interfacing with the tensor network elements, denoted as WW, as illustrated in Fig. S1(c). The value of WW controls the bandwidth of information flow from the neural network to the tensor network. In the NN-fTNS models shown in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 of the main text, WW is chosen to be proportional to the fTNS bond dimension DD. As discussed and demonstrated in Fig. 4 of the main text, increasing WW can lead to a modest improvement in the performance of NN-fTNS, at the cost of enlarging the sizes of the weight matrices W1[i]W_{1}^{[i]} and W2[i]W_{2}^{[i]} with scaling dim(y)×W\dim(y)\times W and W×dim(T[i])W\times\dim(T^{[i]}), respectively.

S-1.2 Other NN based models

We summarize below the architectural details of the various NN-based models used in Fig. 2 of the main text.

For the pure NN model, we replace the fTNS structure in Fig. S1(a) with a two-layer MLP employing a shifted hyperbolic sine activation function, f⁡(x)=sinh⁡(x)+1f(x)=\sinh(x)+1 [64], which directly outputs a real scalar value NN⁡(n)\mathrm{NN}(n) representing the amplitude for configuration |n⟩|n\rangle. In VMC optimization, the pure NN model parameters are initialized randomly.

For the NN-SD model, we follow the standard neural network backflow construction [5, 61, 53], replacing the fTNS in Fig. S1 with a single-particle orbital matrix Mi,k∈ℝNo×NeM_{i,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{o}\times N_{e}}, where NoN_{o} denotes the total number of spin orbitals and NeN_{e} is the total number of electrons. Given a configuration |n⟩|n\rangle, the NN modifies the orbital matrix to produce a configuration-dependent matrix M⁡(n)M(n). The rows of M⁡(n)M(n) corresponding to the occupied orbitals in |n⟩|n\rangle are selected to form a square matrix, whose determinant det(Mio,j)\det(M_{i_{o},j}) yields the final amplitude, where ioi_{o} labels the occupied orbitals. In VMC optimization, the NN-SD is initialized by first fully optimizing the Slater determinant orbital matrix (via minimizing its mean-field energy in the FH model), after which the NN parameters are initialized such that the neural network introduces only small perturbations to the fully optimized Slater determinant. The specific NN structures used are (1) NN-SD (MLP): a two-layer multilayer perceptron; (2) NN-SD (ViT): a Vision Transformer [52] as shown in Fig. S1(a); (3) a convolutional neural network [57, 65].

For the fPEPS×\timesNN-Jastrow model, given a configuration |n⟩|n\rangle and an fPEPS state |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle, we apply the pure NN model to compute a scalar factor NN⁡(n)\mathrm{NN}(n), which is multiplied with the fPEPS amplitude to obtain the final amplitude NN⁡(n)×⟨n|Ψ⟩\mathrm{NN}(n)\times\langle n|\Psi\rangle. In VMC optimization, the fTNS tensors are initialized using SU, and the NN model parameters are initialized randomly.

S-1.3 VMC optimization curves for various Ansätze

We show below an example of our VMC optimization procedure for various Ansätze on a small 4×24\times 2 FH model. We can see the NN-fPEPS model requires fewer VMC optimization steps (around 500 steps) to converge than the NN-SD model (at least 1000 steps).

Appendix S-2 S-2. Tensor network variational monte carlo

S-2.1 a. Variational Monte Carlo

Here we provide a brief review of the variational Monte Carlo algorithm employed in this work, following the presentation in Refs. [6, 60, 44].

In VMC, operator expectation values are estimated via importance sampling of configurations |n⟩=|n1,…,nN⟩|n\rangle=|n_{1},\dots,n_{N}\rangle, where NN is the system size. The energy of a Hamiltonian HH is evaluated as

E=⟨Ψ|H|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩=1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩​∑n|⟨n|Ψ⟩|2​⟨n|H|Ψ⟩⟨n|Ψ⟩=⟨El​o​c​(n)⟩n∼p⁡(n)E=\frac{\langle\Psi|H|\Psi\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}=\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\sum_{n}|\langle n|\Psi\rangle|^{2}\frac{\langle n|H|\Psi\rangle}{\langle n|\Psi\rangle}=\bigl\langle E_{loc}(n)\bigr\rangle_{n\sim p(n)} (S8)

where p⁡(n)=|⟨n|Ψ⟩|2/⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩p(n)=|\langle n|\Psi\rangle|^{2}/\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle and the local energy is defined as

El​o​c​(n)=⟨n|H|Ψ⟩⟨n|Ψ⟩=∑n′⟨n|H|n′⟩​⟨n′|Ψ⟩⟨n|Ψ⟩.E_{loc}(n)=\frac{\langle n|H|\Psi\rangle}{\langle n|\Psi\rangle}=\sum_{n^{\prime}}\langle n|H|n^{\prime}\rangle\,\frac{\langle n^{\prime}|\Psi\rangle}{\langle n|\Psi\rangle}. (S9)

We note that for a local Hamiltonian HH containing O⁡(N)O(N) local terms — for example, the Fermi-Hubbard model considered in this work — each configuration |n⟩|n\rangle is connected to O⁡(N)O(N) configurations |n′⟩|n^{\prime}\rangle with non-zero matrix elements ⟨n|H|n′⟩\langle n|H|n^{\prime}\rangle. Due to the locality of the Fermi-Hubbard model, |n⟩|n\rangle and |n′⟩|n^{\prime}\rangle differ at most on two neighboring sites. The energy is then estimated stochastically as the sample mean of Eloc​(n)E_{\mathrm{loc}}(n) over configurations nn drawn from p⁡(n)p(n) using standard Markov chain sampling with the Metropolis algorithm. To generate new configurations, we employ the sequential nearest-neighbor spin-pair exchange algorithm [60], which preserves the total spin SzS_{z} quantum number during the sampling.

The energy gradient can similarly be evaluated using Monte Carlo sampling:

g=∂E∂θ\displaystyle g=\frac{\partial E}{\partial\theta} =1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩∑n|⟨n|Ψ⟩|2(⟨∂θΨ|n⟩⟨Ψ|n⟩)⋅El​o​c(n)−⟨Ψ|H|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩⋅1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩∑n|⟨n|Ψ⟩|2⟨∂θΨ|n⟩⟨Ψ|n⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\sum_{n}|\langle n|\Psi\rangle|^{2}\,\bigl(\frac{\langle\partial_{\theta}\Psi|n\rangle}{\langle\Psi|n\rangle}\bigr)\cdot E_{loc}(n)-\frac{\langle\Psi|H|\Psi\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\cdot\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\sum_{n}|\langle n|\Psi\rangle|^{2}\,\frac{\langle\partial_{\theta}\Psi|n\rangle}{\langle\Psi|n\rangle} (S10)
=⟨El​o​c​(n)⋅vθ​(n)⟩n∼p⁡(n)−⟨El​o​c​(n)⟩n∼p⁡(n)⋅⟨vθ​(n)⟩n∼p⁡(n)\displaystyle=\bigl\langle E_{loc}(n)\cdot v_{\theta}(n)\bigr\rangle_{n\sim p(n)}-\bigl\langle E_{loc}(n)\bigr\rangle_{n\sim p(n)}\cdot\bigl\langle v_{\theta}(n)\bigr\rangle_{n\sim p(n)} (S11)

where vθ​(n)=⟨∂θΨ|n⟩/⟨Ψ|n⟩v_{\theta}(n)=\langle\partial_{\theta}\Psi|n\rangle/\langle\Psi|n\rangle denotes the logarithmic derivative of the amplitude with respect to the model parameters θ\theta.

The variational state |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle is optimized toward the ground state by gradient descent using stochastic reconfiguration (SR) optimization [66, 67, 68]. In SR, the model parameter update direction is preconditioned by the quantum geometric tensor (QGT) [69], projecting the energy gradient along the direction of imaginary time evolution on the variational manifold. The parameter change d​θ\mathrm{d}\theta is obtained by solving the linear system:

R​d​θd​τ=(S+η​I)​d​θd​τ=−g,\displaystyle R\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}\tau}=(S+\eta\,I)\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}\tau}=-g, (S12)

where R=S+η​IR=S+\eta I, d​τ\mathrm{d}\tau is a small positive time step, SS is the QGT, and η​I\eta I is a small diagonal shift introduced to stabilize the linear solver. Solving the equation yields

d​θ=−(R−1​g)​d​τ,\mathrm{d}\theta=-(R^{-1}g)\,\mathrm{d}\tau, (S13)

where R−1​gR^{-1}g is the SR preconditioned gradient along the imaginary time evolution direction on the variational manifold. The QGT SS is estimated via Monte Carlo sampling as

Si​j=⟨vθi∗​(n)​vθj​(n)⟩n∼p⁡(n)−⟨vθi∗​(n)⟩n∼p⁡(n)​⟨vθj​(n)⟩n∼p⁡(n)S_{ij}=\bigl\langle v_{\theta_{i}}^{*}(n)\,v_{\theta_{j}}(n)\bigr\rangle_{n\sim p(n)}-\bigl\langle v_{\theta_{i}}^{*}(n)\bigr\rangle_{n\sim p(n)}\bigl\langle v_{\theta_{j}}(n)\bigr\rangle_{n\sim p(n)} (S14)

SR can be viewed as a stochastic realization of the imaginary time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) [70]. Finally, model parameters are updated via gradient descent using the preconditioned gradient, θ→θ−γ​R−1​g\theta\to\theta-\gamma R^{-1}g, where γ\gamma denotes the learning rate. In this work, we adopt a dynamic step size schedule, decaying γ\gamma from 0.050.05 to 0.010.01 over the course of the VMC training.

In all of our VMC calculations, the neural networks and the fermionic bias (either Slater determinant or fTNS) are optimized jointly during the variational optimization.

S-2.2 b. Partial tensor network contraction reuse

In Markov Chain VMC calculations, a sequence of configurations that differ locally is typically generated, for example, during the evaluation of local energies for a local Hamiltonian. In the boundary-MPS contraction of TN amplitudes corresponding to these configurations, a significant portion of the computation—associated with partial TN contractions—can be reused, as illustrated in Fig. S3.

As shown in Fig. S3(a), for a pure fTNS, each local tensor depends only on its on-site configuration. Consequently, modifying the configurations in the third row does not affect the environment tensor networks ⟨E2|\langle E_{2}| and |E4⟩|E_{4}\rangle, which can thus be reused for contracting amplitudes ⟨E2|O^3|E4⟩\langle E_{2}|\hat{O}_{3}|E_{4}\rangle that differ solely in the third-row tensors.

In contrast, as shown in Fig. S3(b), for a NN-fPEPS with finite neural network range RR (with R=1R=1 illustrated), each local tensor depends not only on its own configuration but also on those of neighboring sites within range RR. Consequently, configuration changes in the third row also affect tensors in the second and fourth rows. The environment tensor networks ⟨E1|\langle E_{1}| and |E5⟩|E_{5}\rangle remain unaffected and can be reused for contracting amplitudes ⟨E1|O^2​O^3​O^4|E5⟩\langle E_{1}|\hat{O}_{2}\hat{O}_{3}\hat{O}_{4}|E_{5}\rangle, where only the tensors in rows 2 to 4 are varied.

Appendix S-3 S-3. Quantum state fitting

As a supplement to the main text and to further demonstrate the enhanced expressivity of NN-fPEPS, we perform supervised wavefunction optimization (SWO) [71, 33] for quantum state learning. In this approach, we stochastically fit an NN-fPEPS with bond dimension D=4D=4 to a pure fPEPS with a larger bond dimension D=8D=8, by minimizing the negative logarithmic fidelity loss:

ℒ=−log⁡F=−log⁡⟨Ψθ|Φt⟩​⟨Φt|Ψθ⟩⟨Ψθ|Ψθ⟩​⟨Φt|Φt⟩\mathcal{L}=-\log F=-\log\frac{\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\Phi_{t}\rangle\langle\Phi_{t}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle\langle\Phi_{t}|\Phi_{t}\rangle} (S15)

where |Ψθ⟩|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle denotes the NN-fPEPS and |Φt⟩|\Phi_{t}\rangle represents the target pure fPEPS. For comparison, we also perform fitting using a pure fPEPS of the same bond dimension D=4D=4.

We observe a clear separation in the quantum state fitting loss curves: NN-fPEPS rapidly achieves higher fidelity compared to the pure fPEPS, explicitly demonstrating its superior expressivity; see Fig. S4.

Appendix S-4 S-4. Computational cost analysis

For the pure fTNS model and NN-fTNS model without TN contraction reuse, the computational cost of each VMC optimization step scales quadratically as O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) with system size NN. The contraction of a single-layer amplitude ⟨n|Ψ⟩\langle n|\Psi\rangle has cost O⁡(N)O(N), which is the dominant cost in the computation of NN-fTNS amplitudes. Each VMC iteration mainly consists of two parts: sampling new configurations and computing local energies. In the sequential exchange sampling algorithm adopted in this work [60], one sequential sweep over the system requires O⁡(N)O(N) local configuration updates to generate a new configuration. Each local update, without TN contraction reuse, has cost O⁡(N)O(N), leading to an overall sampling cost of O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) per sweep. For local Hamiltonians such as the Fermi-Hubbard model, computing the local energy for a given configuration |n⟩|n\rangle requires evaluating amplitudes for O⁡(N)O(N) connected configurations |nc⟩|n_{c}\rangle, where ⟨nc|H|n⟩≠0\langle n_{c}|H|n\rangle\neq 0, again leading to O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) cost when TN contraction reuse is not employed. Including the cost of boundary-MPS contraction for a single-layer amplitude TN, which scales as O⁡(D4​χ2)O(D^{4}\chi^{2}) (with DD the fTNS bond dimension and χ\chi the auxiliary bond dimension), and adopting the typical choice χ=O⁡(D)\chi=O(D), the total leading cost per VMC step becomes O⁡(M​D6​N2)O(MD^{6}N^{2}) [19], where MM denotes the Monte Carlo sample size.

In practice, the VMC sampling can be efficiently parallelized by distributing multiple Markov chains across CPU cores in an MPI program, reducing the wall-clock time to O⁡(M​D6​N2/Nchain)O(MD^{6}N^{2}/N_{\mathrm{chain}}), where NchainN_{\mathrm{chain}} is the number of parallel chains. In this work, we typically use MM of a few tens of thousands and Nchain≈500N_{\mathrm{chain}}\approx 500.

For fTNS based models where local tensors only have local configuration dependence, partial TN contraction can be reused for computation of related amplitudes, as illustrated in Fig.S3. For pure fTNS, this reuse strategy allows the VMC cost to be reduced from O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) to nearly O⁡(N)O(N) in principle. For example, in the computation of the local energy for a configuration |n⟩|n\rangle using boundary MPS contraction, one may first cache all partial TN contraction intermediates (environment MPS |Ei⟩|E_{i}\rangle in Fig.S3) for ⟨n|Ψ⟩\langle n|\Psi\rangle. Then, to compute ⟨nc|Ψ⟩\langle n_{c}|\Psi\rangle for a locally connected configuration |nc⟩|n_{c}\rangle, only a three-row TN ⟨Ei−1|O^i|Ei+1⟩\langle E_{i-1}|\hat{O}_{i}|E_{i+1}\rangle needs to be contracted, which scales as O⁡(N)O(\sqrt{N}) for a square lattice. If additional TN reuse along the column direction is employed, each |nc⟩|n_{c}\rangle requires contracting only a small plaquette TN with constant cost CncC_{n_{c}} independent of system size, reducing the total cost for local energy evaluation to O⁡(Cnc​N)O(C_{n_{c}}N) [44, 60, 6]. For NN-fTNS models with finite neural network range RR, where each local tensor depends on neighboring configurations within range RR, a similar partial TN contraction reuse scheme can be applied. A comparison of the VMC cost scaling for the above mentioned models as well as conventional fermionic NQS is listed in Table. 1.

As illustrated in Fig. S5 for a 6×66\times 6 square lattice, TN reuse (applied along the row direction) significantly reduces the VMC step cost for pure fPEPS across various bond dimensions, while yielding a more modest cost reduction for NN-fPEPS with neural network range R=1R=1 at larger bond dimensions. We expect the benefit of TN reuse for NN-fPEPS (R=1R=1) to become more pronounced as the system size increases. As discussed in the main text, we emphasize that even employing a minimal finite-range neural network with R=1R=1 yields ground-state energy accuracies that are substantially better than those achieved by pure fTNS.
